lesson.title: Working Together: The Biology of Mutual Benefit
lesson.summary: Mutualism is an interspecific interaction in which both species benefit, and many of the most intricate mutualisms have been shaped over long spans of time by coevolution between the partners.
lesson.body:
So far this unit has focused mostly on competition, an interaction where species are in conflict over a shared resource. But not every interspecific interaction is a contest. Mutualism is an interaction between two different species in which both species benefit, often written using plus and minus notation as a plus slash plus interaction. Both partners come out ahead compared to how they would fare alone, which is quite different from the zero sum feel of competition.

One of the most familiar mutualisms is pollination, the relationship between flowering plants and the bees, and other insects, that visit their flowers. The plant gains a mobile courier that carries pollen from flower to flower, allowing fertilization between individuals that may be far apart. The bee, in turn, gains nectar and pollen, both valuable sources of energy and protein. Neither partner is acting out of altruism. Each is simply pursuing its own survival and reproduction, and the mutual benefit emerges because their needs happen to align. Many flowering plant species have evolved traits, such as particular flower shapes, colors, or scents, that make them more attractive or accessible to their pollinators, while the pollinators in turn may evolve mouthparts or behaviors well suited to those flowers. This kind of back and forth evolutionary shaping between two closely interacting species is called coevolution, and mutualisms are one of the clearest places to see its effects.

A second well documented mutualism, this one in the ocean, is the relationship between clownfish and sea anemones. Sea anemones have stinging cells on their tentacles that deter most fish, but clownfish carry a protective mucus coating that keeps them from being stung, allowing them to live safely among the anemone's tentacles where predators cannot easily follow. The anemone benefits too: clownfish chase away certain anemone eating fish, and their waste products may add nutrients that the anemone can use. Both species have shaped and adjusted to the other over evolutionary time, another likely product of coevolution, though researchers are still working out the full details of how the clownfish's immunity to the sting evolved.

Mutualisms are not always so dramatic or visible. Mycorrhizal fungi form partnerships with the roots of most land plant species, in which the fungus extends a vast network of thin filaments through the soil, gathering water and mineral nutrients like phosphorus far beyond what the plant's own roots could reach, while the plant supplies the fungus with sugars produced through photosynthesis. This kind of quiet, underground mutualism is thought to be one of the reasons plants were able to colonize dry land in the first place, hundreds of millions of years ago. Across all of these examples, from flowers and bees to fungi and roots, the common thread is that both species are measurably better off together than apart, which sets mutualism apart from the two interactions covered next, commensalism and parasitism, where the benefits are far more one sided.
